requested.title: verifyCaptcha has no default difficulty floor, so tokens are fungible across every captcha in the app
mintCaptcha does not range-check a per-call bits value, and a sealed bits <= 0 makes the proof-of-work check a no-op
A negative ageMs is rejected as too-fast even when minAgeMs is 0, locking visitors out of protection mode under clock skew
A bad per-call or configured minAgeMs is reported as a captcha:minAgeMs filter fault
MemoryNonceStore iterates the entire map on every consume, making the default replay store quadratic
SqliteNonceStore opens the database without WAL or a busy_timeout, in the exact configuration the docs recommend for multi-instance deploys
SqliteNonceStore never creates its parent directory, and the failed lazy construction is not cached so it 500s on every request
minAgeMs, maxAgeMs, store and storePath are not validated, and a NaN maxAgeMs silently disables token expiry
MochiCaptchaOptions.bits is documented as defaulting to 16 while the real default is 19, and both widgets default the prop to 16

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: Verified mechanically. `CAPTCHA_AAD` is the module-level constant `'mochi-captcha'` (pow.ts:5), used identically at mint (captcha.ts:50) and verify (captcha.ts:66), so every captcha token in an app decrypts at every captcha-protected endpoint — there is no per-endpoint scope anywhere in the sealed payload (`{ iat, nonce, bits }`). verifyCaptcha then honours the sealed `bits` at L111 and the only floor is `options?.minBits !== undefined && bits < options.minBits` at L84-86, which is skipped entirely when the caller omits it. I confirmed the framework knows this matters: Mochi.ts:1786 passes `minBits: protectionOptions.bits` with a comment saying exactly why, and clearance.ts applies the same `bits < minBits` idea to clearance cookies. I grepped the whole repo for `minBits` — it appears only in Mochi.ts:1785-1786 and captcha.test.ts:357-367, and I read all of 150-captcha.md: the Options table lists only bits/minAgeMs/maxAgeMs/store/storePath and the API table shows `verifyCaptcha(formData, options?)` without enumerating options, so `minBits` is genuinely undiscoverable for an app author. The concrete attack holds: an app that mints cheap tokens on one form (`mintCaptcha({ bits: 12 })`, a pattern 152-protection.md:122 itself teaches) and expensive ones on another has its expensive form silently accept the cheap tokens, cutting the intended work by 2^(delta). packages/site/src/routes.ts:261 confirms harvesting is trivial — `/api/captcha-demo/mint` is an unauthenticated JSON endpoint returning a fresh token (rate-limited 60/min). The one thing I'd narrow: the exposure only exists in a mixed-difficulty app (a uniform-`bits` app is unaffected, since all tokens then cost the same), and no identity or authorization boundary is crossed — only proof-of-work cost. I'm keeping MEDIUM because this is precisely the constant-AAD / unscoped-capability-token pattern the project's own threat model asks reviewers to flag, and the fix (default `minBits` to the verifying runtime's `bits`) is a pure improvement.

The code path is exactly as described. captcha.ts:45 is `const bits = options?.bits ?? resolved.bits;` with no validation — nullish coalescing preserves `0` — and the value is sealed at L50 unchecked. The 1-32 integer bound in config.ts:33-35 guards only the `Mochi.serve({ captcha: { bits } })` path (and, per the comment at config.ts:31, the `captcha:bits` filter, which is applied *before* the bound deliberately); it never sees a per-call mint. verifyCaptcha re-reads the sealed value with only `typeof parsed.bits !== 'number'` (L76) and then evaluates `leadingZeroBits(digest) < bits` at L111, so with `bits: 0` the comparison is `>=0 < 0`, always false, and the proof-of-work check is unconditionally satisfied — including for `pow === ''`, since L65 coerces a missing field to the empty string and `powInput` happily hashes it. I confirmed the asymmetry the finding leans on: `solveBudgetMs`, resolved two lines later, IS validated at L47-49, and captcha.test.ts:150-153 has `test('rejects a non-positive per-mint solve budget')` with no bits counterpart. I also verified the inverted failure mode in the widgets: MochiCaptcha.svelte:116 and MochiCaptchaAuto.svelte:108 both reject `bits < 1` in `validateProps`, mark it non-retryable, and in production `suppressed` collapses the whole `{#if mounted && !suppressed}` block — including the two hidden inputs at L374-375 — to a blank spacer, so real visitors submit no token at all while a scripted post with a token and empty pow passes. The fractional case checks out too: `bits: 0.5` accepts any digest whose first byte is < 128, i.e. ~half of nonces. And `NaN` does fail closed, because `JSON.stringify` writes `null` and the `typeof` guard at L76 rejects it. I'm downgrading to BUG rather than MEDIUM because `bits` is set only by application code — an attacker has no influence over it (the token is AES-256-SIV sealed and unforgeable), so reaching the fail-open requires a developer bug, and that bug simultaneously blocks every legitimate submission, which makes it loud rather than silent. It remains a genuine missing-validation/fail-open gap worth closing in both mintCaptcha and verifyCaptcha.

Confirmed in code. `ageMs = Date.now() - iat` at L89 is never clamped, and the floor check at L100 is an unconditional `if (ageMs < minAgeMs) return reject('too-fast', …)`. With `minAgeMs === 0` any negative age is refused, and a zero floor enforces nothing, so the rejection buys no security — a negative age cannot indicate tampering, because `iat` is inside the AEAD-sealed payload and an attacker cannot move it. Mochi.ts:1786 is the framework's own and only `minAgeMs: 0` caller (`verifyCaptcha(formData, { minAgeMs: 0, minBits: protectionOptions.bits })`), so protection mode is exactly where this lands. I traced the client consequence: MochiCaptchaAuto.svelte `submit()` hits `!res.ok` on the 403, calls `failWith(detail)` with the default `retryable = true`, which increments the sessionStorage counter (L89-95) and latches `phase = 'exhausted'` at `maxAttempts` (default 5, resolveProtectionOptions), and `onMount` re-reads the counter at L125 so reloads stay exhausted. The authors' comment at L91-93 argues only against *padding* a positive floor (subtracting an allowance wider than minAgeMs would delete the check) — it does not address the case where there is no floor at all. The strongest evidence this is an oversight rather than a decision is the handled mirror case: clearance.ts:39 returns `ageMs >= -CLEARANCE_DRIFT_ALLOWANCE_MS && ageMs < maxAgeMs`, and protection.test.ts:87-90 has a dedicated test, 'a slightly-future clearance from a fast-clocked instance is accepted'. There is no equivalent test or tolerance for the captcha token. Two caveats keep this at BUG: it needs a multi-instance deploy without sticky routing (or a backward clock step) with skew exceeding the solve time — mint and verify landing on the same instance makes `ageMs` exact — and 150-captcha.md:185 shows the authors expect negative `ageMs` to occur in the field; also 'locked out with no path forward' is a little strong, since the counter is per-tab sessionStorage and a new tab clears it.

Straightforwardly confirmed by reading L95-98. The effective floor is `options?.minAgeMs ?? applyFilter('captcha:minAgeMs', resolved.minAgeMs, …)`, so it can come from three sources: the per-call option (which short-circuits the filter entirely — captcha.test.ts:348-353 has a test asserting exactly that bypass), the filter, or the configured default. The throw at L96-98 is unconditional and always blames the filter: `Captcha: the captcha:minAgeMs filter returned ${minAgeMs}`. I verified both misattribution paths concretely. (1) `verifyCaptcha(formData, { minAgeMs: 1_000_000 })` in an app with no filter registered: `limitMs = 900_000 + 30_000 = 930_000`, so `1_000_000 >= limitMs` trips the guard and the operator is told a nonexistent filter misbehaved. (2) A configured `minAgeMs: NaN` slips resolveCaptchaOptions, because its only guard is `minAgeMs >= maxAgeMs` and `NaN >= 900_000` is false; it then fails `Number.isFinite` here, at request time, again naming a phantom filter. The existing test (captcha.test.ts:331-336) only exercises the genuine filter case, which is why the misattribution was never noticed. This is purely a diagnostics/developer-experience defect — no security impact, no behavioural change in the accept/reject decision — so BUG is the right severity, and the finding's own 'high' confidence is justified.

The algorithmic claim is exactly right: `consume()` walks every entry in `this.seen` (L11-15) before each insert, so one successful verification costs O(n) and sustained traffic is O(n^2); the walk is synchronous JS and blocks the event loop for all other requests; and in the steady state it usually deletes nothing. 'memory' is the default store (config.ts:59), entries live until `iat + maxAgeMs + driftAllowanceMs` (≈15.5 min with defaults, via `expiresAt` at captcha.ts:117), and there is no cap on the map. The authors' justification at L9-10 ('this map only grows one entry per successful send, so the scan stays tiny') is an assumption about volume, not an invariant. The finding's supporting evidence is accurate — I read nonceStore.test.ts:77-89 and it is precisely `test('prunes via an index rather than scanning the table')`, asserting `USING INDEX nonces_expires_at` and `not.toContain('SCAN nonces')` for the SQLite store, i.e. the authors engineered away in SQLite exactly the scan the memory store performs. I'm downgrading from MEDIUM to BUG on exploitability. I traced the insert path in verifyCaptcha: `store.consume` at L118 runs only after minBits, the age floor, the expiry bound and the PoW check all pass, so every entry costs the attacker a genuine 2^bits solve (2^19 by default) plus one mint request and one submit request. That makes the economics backwards for a DoS: the attacker pays tens of milliseconds of CPU per entry, and the server's per-consume walk only approaches that cost once n reaches the millions, which requires roughly a hundred cores sustained for the full 15.5-minute window while simultaneously pushing thousands of requests per second at the app — at which point the flood, not the Map walk, is the problem. The unbounded growth (no ceiling, so memory is attacker-influenced) is arguably the more real half. Worth fixing as the finding recommends (insertion-ordered head-shifting plus a hard cap), but it is a scalability/robustness defect rather than a practical availability vulnerability.

Every factual element checks out. The constructor (L27-33) is `new Database(path, { create: true })` followed only by two DDL statements — no pragmas at all. I confirmed against Bun's own documentation (bun.com/docs/runtime/sqlite, 'WAL mode') that WAL is not the default and must be enabled with `db.run("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;")`, and found no documented default `busy_timeout` anywhere in the Bun docs; SQLite's own default is no busy handler, so a losing writer gets SQLITE_BUSY immediately. Meanwhile `consume()` takes two separate implicit write transactions on every call — an unconditional `DELETE … WHERE expires_at < ?` at L39 then the `INSERT OR IGNORE` at L40 — and in rollback-journal mode each commit fsyncs under an EXCLUSIVE whole-database lock. The configuration this breaks is the one the docs prescribe: 150-captcha.md:195 says 'Use `store: 'sqlite'` with shared storage' for multi-instance deploys, which means several processes writing one file (and on NFS/EFS, SQLite's advisory locking is unreliable outright). I verified the error propagation: neither `store.consume` at captcha.ts:118 nor `consumeCaptcha` at captcha.ts:151 is wrapped, so a SQLITE_BUSY throw escapes the application's form action. I also confirmed the cited precedent precisely — grepping every `new Database(` in the repo returns exactly two file-backed opens, and support/src/db.server.ts:69 is the only one that runs `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`, making SqliteNonceStore the lone sqlite store in the project without it. BUG is the right severity: this is an availability/robustness defect under concurrency, not a boundary bypass. My only residual uncertainty is whether bun:sqlite sets an undocumented internal busy_timeout; the WAL half is certain regardless, and the absence of any pragma is the substance of the finding.

Confirmed on all three legs. (1) `new Database(path, { create: true })` at L28 creates the file but not its parent directories — SQLite returns SQLITE_CANTOPEN for a missing directory — and this repo states it outright: support/src/db.server.ts:67 carries the comment 'bun:sqlite won't create the parent directory.' immediately above its own `mkdirSync`. (2) The cited precedents are real: queue.ts:492 is `mkdirSync(path.dirname(path.resolve(file)), { recursive: true })` before constructing the SQL handle, and cache-storage.ts:301 does `mkdirSync(this.directory, { recursive: true })`; SqliteNonceStore does neither. (3) The non-cached-failure amplification is real: config.ts:73-83 assigns `g[GLOBAL_KEY] = runtime` only after `createStore(resolved)` returns, so a throwing constructor leaves the global unset and the construction is retried — and rethrown — on every subsequent request. I verified the boot-vs-request timing claim too: grepping `getCaptchaRuntime` shows the only non-captcha.ts caller is Mochi.ts:672, guarded by `protectionEnabled && options.protection`, and `resolveCaptchaOptions` is reachable only through `getCaptchaRuntime`. So with protection off, the runtime (and the store) is built lazily on the first `mintCaptcha` during a page render, and a bad `storePath` yields a clean startup followed by an unending stream of 500s. The default path is safe — Mochi.ts:602 mkdirs outDir subdirectories, so `.mochi/` exists — which correctly scopes this to a custom `storePath` with a missing parent (e.g. `data/nonces.sqlite`), a configuration the support app exposes directly via its `CAPTCHA_NONCE_DB` env var. BUG severity is right; both recommendations (mkdir in the constructor, validate the store eagerly at boot) follow existing in-repo patterns.

I walked each sub-claim through the code. resolveCaptchaOptions bounds-checks `bits` (L33-35), `driftAllowanceMs` (L44-46) and `solveBudgetMs` (L50-52) but not `minAgeMs`, `maxAgeMs`, `store` or `storePath`, and because every NaN comparison is false the single remaining guard at L38 (`minAgeMs >= maxAgeMs`) is porous in both directions. (1) `maxAgeMs: NaN`: `2000 >= NaN` is false so it passes; at verify `limitMs = NaN + 30_000 = NaN`, the L96 guard is also bypassed (`2000 >= NaN` is false, and `Number.isFinite(2000)` holds), and the expiry test `ageMs > limitMs` is then always false — token expiry is silently off. `expiresAt = iat + NaN = NaN`, so MemoryNonceStore's `exp < now` prune never fires and the map grows without bound, while SqliteNonceStore binds a non-finite value against `expires_at INTEGER NOT NULL` and throws (SQLite stores NaN as NULL). (2) `minAgeMs: NaN` likewise clears L38 and surfaces only at request time as the misattributed filter error at captcha.ts:97 — which is the same defect F4 covers from the other file. (3) `store` is unvalidated and createStore's fallthrough at L92 returns it verbatim, so a bogus literal becomes a request-time `store.consume is not a function` TypeError rather than a boot error; TypeScript blocks this for typed callers, so it needs JS or a cast, and it does fail closed. The cited real-world evidence is accurate: support/src/index.ts:55-58 hand-rolls `Number(env) || DEFAULT`, an explicit `Number.isFinite(...)` ternary, and a literal-union narrowing — exactly the guards the framework omits — and that app's own hole is real too, since `Number('')` is `0` and finite, so `CAPTCHA_MIN_AGE_MS=""` drops the production support form's timing floor to zero. BUG is correct: the security control (expiry) genuinely disappears, but only via an application passing a non-finite value, which `Number(process.env.X)` on an unset variable makes a plausible mistake rather than an attacker-reachable one.

Verified against source and git history. types.ts:9 reads 'Proof-of-work difficulty in leading zero bits. Default: 16.' while config.ts:27 defines `DEFAULT_CAPTCHA_BITS = 19`; packages/mochi/src/types.ts:705 repeats the stale value ('Default: 16 bits, a 2s floor, a 15-minute expiry, and an in-memory nonce store'), and 150-captcha.md correctly states 19 in both its Options table (L163) and its Props table (L98). Git confirms the drift: `git log -S 'Default: 16.'` on captcha/types.ts points at e7335002, the original captcha commit, and `git show 5028c6b6^:…/config.ts` shows the pre-change code was `const bits = o.bits ?? 16;` — so commit 5028c6b6 raised the default to 19 and left the JSDoc and both widget prop defaults behind. MochiCaptcha.svelte:12 and MochiCaptchaAuto.svelte:11 are still `bits = 16`. The functional consequence the finding draws is sound: a developer writing `<MochiCaptcha token={captcha.token} />` instead of spreading `{...captcha}` gets a widget that brute-forces for 16 leading zeros, sets `verified = true`, submits, and is rejected at captcha.ts:111 roughly 7 times in 8 (a 16-bit solution has a 1/8 chance of also clearing 19), collapsing into the deliberately generic 'Verification failed' message with the real cause only on the `captcha:verify` event. I checked the framework's own call sites are unaffected — templates/ProtectionShell/ProtectionShell.svelte passes `{bits}` explicitly from the minted result. Note the mismatch fails closed, not open (the widget under-solves and is refused), so this is a documentation/consistency footgun rather than a security weakness; BUG and the finding's 'high' confidence are both right, and the recommendation to reference DEFAULT_CAPTCHA_BITS instead of a literal is the correct fix.
